It struck me earlier today, in the wake of browsing a couple of threads about asset forfeiture, and after following a fairly long train of thought, that the single-minded focus on STEM subjects in the modern world likely is part of the problem rather than part of the solution.

Here's the way it unfolded -

The first thing that got me thinking in that direction was the realization of just how little human society has advanced in... well... all of history, really. Specifically - I've noted in the past, just by way of negative comparison, how similar modern asset forfeiture policies are to the Middle Ages practice of a lord allowing his mercenaries to plunder conquered territories. It's really the same basic strategy - the lord maintains the loyalty of his hired thugs by giving them license to loot and pillage "the spoils of war."

But the thing that really struck me thinking about that this morning is the bald fact that that means that our current society is essentially duplicating a policy that was already recognizably destructive at least a millennia ago. So in 1000 years, we haven't even managed to advance far enough philosophically or ethically to outgrow even that blatantly despicable practice. And that's just the tip of the iceberg - when one stops and looks, our civilization is littered from top to bottom with ideas and beliefs and views that haven't changed in at least a millennia.

And I can only conclude that that's at the heart of much of our current difficulties. We've made enormous strides in science and technology over the centuries, but philosophically we really haven't progressed much, if at all. We've really simply just gone from primitive tribalists with spears and swords to primitive tribalists with rocket launchers and drones.

We don't need to focus on technology. Technology has already far outstripped philosophy. We don't even understand ourselves well enough to manage what we already have. Hell - we're really no different from those dark age barbarians that couldn't even be trusted with the ability to work metal without someone deciding that the thing to do was to fashion it into the most efficient killing machines possible so that he could get a bunch of ignorant peasants to go kill another bunch of ignorant peasants so that he could expand his kingdom and get some better food and a few more mistresses. The only thing that's changed is the technology available to the lord of the manor, and thus the efficiency of the killing machines he will cause to be made.

No - what humanity really needs is to advance philosophically to at least something resembling the degree to which we've already advanced technologically. What we really need is to be able to think clearly enough and rationally enough - not just individually, here and there, in little circlejerky pockets, but broadly and generally - to manage what we already have.

Yet here we are, in a world in which all are urged to pursue STEM degrees.

---

For further consideration:

Is that an accident? I find it a bit too convenient that sufficient advancement philosophically would rob the lord of the manor of his ill-gotten power, and the society from which he draws that power has been taught to demean such a pursuit, and to instead glorify the pursuit of that which makes the lord's killing machines more efficient.

It's particularly easy to demean "social sciences" since they're so much the domain of idiots and crackpots. I think the case could be made though that that's not a reflection of the "social sciences" themselves, but of our attitude toward them. Any thing that's widely derided and vilified by "serious people" is likely destined to become the domain of idiots and crackpots, since they're the ones most likely to have the least fear of being judged harshly by the gibbering hordes.

Aaaand... I guess that's about it for this one. It's now where I wanted it - in print and in at least some sort of order.
